newsitem.title: PERU: Fujimori tours tunnels that inspired hostage raid.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori tours tunnels that inspired hostage raid.

text.p: A jubilant President Alberto Fujimori led Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda on Saturday around the 3,000-year-old tunnel ruins that inspired Peru's ingenious raid on rebel hostage-takers.

Fujimori, buoyed by soaring popularity after rescuing all but one of the 72 hostages alive from the Japanese ambassador's house, said the tunnels his troops used to overrun the house owed their inspiration to the great Chavin de Huantar ruins.

"One early morning three months ago I woke suddenly and thought that if a peaceful solution was not possible, an option would be this kind of network of tunnels," said Fujimori after emerging from the ruins' underground labyrinth.

Sixty men working 24 hours a day spent three months and shifted 200 truckloads of earth to build a warren of tunnels underneath the diplomatic compound in Lima. Like Chavin de Huantar, the military's tunnels included sleeping and eating facilities, as well as food deposits.
Army and navy commandos swarmed through the tunnels and into the besieged residence on Tuesday in a melee of explosions and gunfire, overwhelming the 14 Tupac Amaru rebels.
As well as captive judge Carlos Giusti, all of the guerrillas and two of the 140 commandos involved in the operation also died.

"The Chavin de Huantar tunnels inspired us, and I give thanks to the ancient gods of the Chavin culture," said Fujimori, laughing and relaxed in jeans as he spoke against a backdrop of towering snow-capped mountains.
Ikeda said the ancient stone tunnels were "incredible, precise and built with great technique" and added his own thanks to the pre-Christian deities that inspired them.

Operation Chavin de Huantar was the code name Fujimori gave the raid, adding a native Peruvian touch to an operation that Fujimori proudly said was planned and executed without any foreign help. "There was no American, British, Israeli or Japanese advice. None at all," he said in an interview with Reuters on Friday.
Peru's Interior Minister General Cesar Saucedo denied reports that two Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels were summarily executed by troops in the raid.
"All of them died in combat," he told Reuters, adding that the reports came from "people who want to cloud the success of the operation."
But asked about reports that some of the rebels were shot while trying to surrender, he said "Who can say?"

The Chavin de Huantar ruins are nestled in a dramatic Andean valley amid jagged peaks in northern Peru's Ancash department. Women working in the fields rose to applaud and wave at Fujimori as he landed in his helicopter, while children swarmed around him and Ikeda.
The elaborate tunnel complex lies beneath a huge ceremonial temple and, in the time of the Chavin culture about 3,000 years ago, could be visited only by a few select priests.

With the government's attention now focused on eradicating the remainder of the MRTA and the more powerful Shining Path insurgency, officials were careful to avoid gloating over their success in freeing the hostages.

"We must be alert," said Saucedo, although he added that "almost nothing" remains of the MRTA and neither group was capable of mounting a repeat of the Dec. 17 storming of the Japanese ambassador's mansion.

The Japanese envoy said Tokyo had not decided if Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto would visit Peru to hear first-hand how Fujimori pulled off the hostage rescue, met with worldwide acclaim and relief.

Ikeda was due to fly out of Peru late on Saturday night accompanied by three of the Japanese ex-hostages, including ambassador Morihisa Aoki, whose ill-fated Dec. 17 cocktail party was stormed by the MRTA.

Fujimori said the tunnel complex of Chavin de Huantar was obviously far superior to the military replica dug out beneath the Japanese diplomatic compound. "Why don't you make a new Japanese embassy here?" he quipped to a laughing Ikeda.

Fujimori's approval rating rocketed from 45 percent the day before the raid to 74 percent two days after, according to a poll by Datum International. The poll, based on 300 interviews, confirmed a massive recovery in the Peruvian leader's popularity, which had dropped to near historic lows in the weeks preceding the assault.
Earlier, Ikeda faulted Peru for not providing better information on guerrilla movements, saying it could have prevented the takeover in the first place.
"Regarding the movements of the MRTA, if we had had information, the crisis could never have happened," he said.

"Generally speaking, the Peruvian government, as the host nation, has the primary responsibility to ensure safety and protect (against terrorism) under the Vienna Treaty," Ikeda said. It was the first hint of an official rebuke from Tokyo for the takeover.
